item.title: Should you marry her?
item.description: Weigh the costs against the benefits
item.content:encoded:
Marriage is a contract: you promise not to break up with your partner even if you later end up wanting to, and they promise the same.1 A wedding is a contract enforcement mechanism: by standing up in front of your community and declaring that you won’t leave each other, you make it harder to back out later. If you break up for frivolous or fixable reasons, your community will judge you. If you go to your friends for advice about your relationship struggles, they’ll be more oriented toward helping you make it work and less likely to suggest you leave.2 Your acquaintances will be less likely to try to tempt you away from your spouse,3 partly because others in your community will think they’re shitty if they do.

The main benefit of marriage is investment.4 When both of you are much more confident that the other will stick around for the long haul,5 you are incentivized to make investments in a joint life that wouldn’t otherwise have been worth it. This could look like buying a house or having a kid, dividing labor like life admin and fixing things and cooking to make joint life more efficient, or putting in the work to understand each other better and meet each other’s needs better.

Beyond that, I’ve found the emotional security of commitment creates room for a more radical trust and love. You allow yourself to sink into each other and extend deep roots in each other’s souls.

The main cost, assuming you plan to get married eventually,6 is that you might have found someone better. So how do you decide whether to commit to your current partner? By popular request, I’ve made up a brief guide. While this advice is gender-neutral, women generally know what they want and are ready to commit sooner than men, so it’s addressed to the confused rat boys in my life.

Once your girlfriend is ready to get married, you have three basic choices at any given point in time:

  • Commit to her now: pay the cost of forgone options, get the benefit of investment.

  • Break up with her now: pay the cost of searching for someone new, get the benefit of a different (and hopefully better) marriage starting in a few years.

  • Wait and see: pay the cost of delaying the start of marriage (and thus the accumulation of investment benefits), get the benefit of more information to make a better decision.

The first question is how long you should wait and see. A rough model is that you learn one more unit of information about your compatibility with your partner from every doubling of the amount of time you spend with them. My husband and I dated for about ~2.5 years before getting engaged, and we spent maybe 15 hours a week actively hanging out together over that period.7 So we’d already spent ~2000 full-time-equivalent hours together, or ~11 doublings starting from our first hour. A fifty year marriage would have been ~40,000 more hours, only another ~4-5 doublings on top of what we had already experienced (and as I’ll discuss below our marriage will probably be a fair bit shorter than that).

In general, if you’ve been with someone for a couple of years already, there’s not much point hanging around longer generically waiting for more information. You should have some understanding of what exactly you’re hoping to learn in another six months,8 and pay attention to make sure you’re actually learning something about that.

The second question is how your girlfriend compares to other women you could marry. Your wife will fulfill three main roles in your life:

  • Cofounder: Your wife will build a life with you. At a minimum, you’ll handle household maintenance and life admin together. Beyond that, what exactly you build together will vary — my marriage has revolved around working together to have impact, many are oriented around raising children, some are about creating rich shared experiences — so what you need from a cofounder will vary. But broadly speaking, you’ll want to feel like she’s competent and on top of her shit, that she’s bringing a lot to the table and your skillsets complement each other well,9 and that you communicate well and resolve differences constructively.

  • Friend: You’ll hang out with your wife more than you hang out with any other person. You’ll want to be able to laugh easily together, have a lot to talk about with each other, and do things together that you both enjoy.

  • Lover: Your wife will be the primary outlet for your romantic and sexual drives. You’ll want to find her charming and hot, you’ll want to be in love with her.

You probably have more evidence lodged in your brain than you appreciate, and some focused and organized introspection can probably move you. For example:

  • For the cofounder role, how excited would you be to literally cofound an organization with your girlfriend? Would you be excited to hire her?10 Would you be excited to work for her? How would she stack up among people you’ve worked closely with? What would her manager and coworkers say about her? Do you trust the way she makes important decisions? Would you trust her advice about your important decisions? What does it feel like to make decisions together and divide up the tasks of life together? If something happens to you, like you get hit by a car or your parent has a stroke and needs a lot of care, does it feel like a relief that she’s around to take care of things? Do you have similar aspirations for the life you want to build and a plan to achieve it together — if you want kids, are you on the same page about how much work each of you is going to put into childcare and do you think she’d be a good mother?

  • For the friend role, how much would you hang out with your girlfriend if it had to just be platonic (where would she rank in the rotation of friends you see every now and then)? What interests and joys do you share? What are the points of connection that seem rarest and most precious? What are the interests and perspectives you don’t share with her that you really wish you did?

  • For the lover role, how attracted were you to your girlfriend in the first twenty minutes of speaking to her, and how often have you had feelings of attraction that strong (and what’s the denominator — how many women have you spoken to for 20 minutes)? How’s the sex in this relationship compared to other sex you’ve had in your life? How strong is your felt sense of love and affection compared to what you felt in previous longer-term relationships?

  • Make a big list of all the women you can think of, whether they’re single or not, and ask your friends to come up with names you might not have known. Based on what you know about them, think about how you think they’d do at each of these roles compared to your girlfriend. For the ones that seem like they would plausibly be better overall than your girlfriend, ask yourself how often that kind of woman tends to come onto the market,11 and ask an honest friend if she’s out of your league. Go to parties and meet some of them, and see how it feels to be around them. Try to quickly falsify some of your hypotheses about them.

The last question is how short is life. How much do you value the next few years of your life, when you could either be married to your current partner or on the prowl for a new one, compared to the future span of your marriage?

Given AI timelines, I think the expected length of your marriage if you get married today is probably something like ten years.12 Even if you want to set that aside,13 I’m skeptical you should think of the remainder of your natural life as worth fifty or sixty times as much as the next year. You probably have some intrinsic time preference (you-in-fifty-years is much less “you” than you-next-year) and you should discount the future to some extent because of uncertainty.14

I’ve tended to think of a normal lifespan as being worth about thirty times as much as next year. That means if it takes three years to find another partner, you’ve spent 10% of the rest of your life searching. This, combined with the investment benefit — which I think could easily be 10% or more over a ten year marriage — means that you need to find someone who’s better than your current partner by a pretty healthy margin to be worth the wait.

I admit I have a conflict of interest in writing this post. I love marriage (I wish I’d gotten married earlier) and want to fit in another wedding or two before the Singularity. And I feel a sense of sisterhood with your girlfriend — I’m not sure you should marry her, but for her sake, I think you can figure it out soon.

1

This is not an absolute promise, and nor should it be. You can and should get divorced if it becomes miserable to be with your partner over a sustained period. But you can’t break up just because you met someone better or otherwise start to think you can find someone better (for example, because you became higher status, or your partner became less attractive, or loses their job). And most importantly, you should stop investing mental energy into the question of whether you could find someone better.

2

And if you do end up getting a divorce, they’ll also know to treat this as a really big deal compared to a normal breakup, something you’re going to grieve over for years.

3

This also applies to secondary partners if you're poly. A poly friend said that being married made dating other people lower-stakes, because everyone was clearer about where they stood in the partner pecking order.

4

There is also an insurance benefit — if you become a much less attractive partner one day, you’ll get to lock in love and affection from someone who would now be way out of your league. But I think this is a smaller benefit in practice, and getting married primarily for the insurance benefit is not a healthy attitude to marriage. You mostly want marriage to make you invest more in becoming a better partner for your spouse, not let yourself go.

5

Just how long a haul that might be is an important question which I’ll get to in a minute.

6

If you don’t really mind being single forever, you can afford to have very high standards, which means a lot of this guide won’t apply.

7

This was unusually intensive, because we lived together for most of the time we were dating and half of that was during the COVID lockdown.

8

For example, maybe you need to have a lot of long conversations sorting out where you stand on kids, like my husband and I did. Or maybe your experience in the relationship so far has been seriously unrepresentative — e.g. you’ve been long distance for a while and just moved to the same city, one or both of you made a major career or lifestyle change, etc.

9

Complementarity is especially valuable if you want to have kids. They are a huge amount of work and it’s a really big deal if your partner is up for doing the lion’s share of that work.

10

You’ll have to modify this somewhat if you do something super technical that she doesn’t have expertise in. But even so, the best cofounders can add a lot in nontechnical roles.

11

In general, the kinds of women who have been married longer tend to be in higher demand and come onto the dating market more rarely.

12

Expectations are longer than medians, which I see as closer to five or six years for top-human-expert dominating AI.

13

For example, maybe you want to make a commitment that you’ll stay with your partner for a subjective period of time equivalent to one ordinary pre-Singularity marriage (e.g. fifty years), even if the Singularity does happen in between. I would strongly discourage you from making commitments that last much longer than that.

14

You shouldn't come into marriage with this attitude, but a relevant point for thinking about the appropriate discount is that not all marriages last fifty or sixty years.

item.title: The Gaang is too old for this
item.content:encoded:
This blog post contains spoilers for Avatar Aang: The Last Airbender, which is a bad movie that’s also not actually out yet.

After languishing in production hell for seven years, the new Avatar movie featuring adult Aang, Katara, et al was unceremoniously leaked on Twitter last month. I compromised my ethics to watch it so you don’t have to.

The plot

The movie opens with an Aang in his mid twenties squirreling away Air Nomad relics in an abandoned Air Temple.1 The latest relic in his growing collection is an extremely old figurine, of a woman named “Sonam.” He gets attacked by a nonbender terrorist cell called The Denied (presumably predecessors of Korra‘s Equalists), who nearly take down the whole temple2 and make away with the statuette, which apparently had a map inside it.

One of Aang’s past lives, an annoying Earthbender Avatar from a zillion years ago, tells him that Sonam was a “lost Avatar,” forgotten by history and inaccessible through standard Avatar meditation. Sonam had a special magic staff with the power to directly channel the Spirit Realm, also lost to the mists of time. Aang infers that the Denied must be after the staff, and presses Earth guy for where it might be; he points Aang to a bigass snowy mountain.

Aang makes off in the middle of the night for the bigass snowy mountain, sending messenger birds to assemble the Gaang to meet him there. At the top is a beefy guy frozen in ice. Aang breaks the guy out, and the whole mountain starts to crumble. As they’re tumbling to their deaths, we discover this guy is an Airbender! And a powerful one — he singlehandedly holds off the falling mountain with a wind beam until Appa shows up with the Gaang to save them all.

The thawed Airbender is named Tagha, and it turns out (surprise!) he was Avatar Sonam’s right hand man. He tells them Sonam’s staff can turn people into Airbenders. Aang is really excited about getting the staff to turn a bunch of people into Airbenders, and also really worried the Denied will get the staff and turn themselves into a bunch of Airbenders, so Tagha and the Gaang head off on a fetch quest in the Fire Lord’s royal airship.

Tagha leads the ship over the Endless Ocean (the far side of the map from the show, believed to have no landmasses) and through a neverending super-tornado (”The Immortal Storm”), where their airship is literally rent apart3 and they all nearly die. Katara is briefly very pissed about this but quickly pipes down.

They finally make it to a cluster of dead Lion Turtle islands where Sonam left her staff, and Aang goes off to try to spiritually connect with Sonam and find her staff. Tagha, who was supposed to stay behind and help the others fix the airship, follows him instead. Katara, who’s well and truly suspicious now, follows Tagha. Turns out (surprise!) he’s evil, and they fight, and he crushes the ship but (surprise!) the others actually escaped and now Katara and Toph and Sokka all fight him, and he smacks them all down with a series of body slams.

By this time Aang has found the staff. Tagha takes it from him and immediately begins bragging about how he killed all his friends. Aang gets pissed, and they fight. Tagha kills Aang with a wind beam and flies off on a mind-controlled Appa. He lands on the deck of the Denied’s airship like a god and gives them all Airbending.

In the spirit world, the dead Aang encounters Avatar Sonam, who tells him that Tagha was corrupted by the horrors of war into wanting to kill all non-Airbenders or something. He stole Sonam’s staff and turned into some kind of superhuman monster, and she just barely managed to lock him away at the top of the bigass mountain, hide away her staff, and haul her temple up into the Spirit World before dying. Sonam tells Aang he has to stop Tagha before he brings the temple back into the real world and connects the staff to it, which will give him untold power.

Aang is then revived by Katara. It turns out they had all died offscreen (!), but Katara was conveniently auto-revived by the extra spiritual waters around the Lion Turtle islands, and then revived everyone else. They all then jump into the mouth of the ocean spirit to enter a portal into the Spirit World to find Tagha. After some wacky shenanigans where they’re all different ages and they encounter an annoying six-eyed board spirit, they make it to Sonam’s temple just as Tagha is transferring it between worlds.

Back in the Earthly realm, Sonam’s temple hovers over Republic City. There’s a big colorful confusing fight in which Aang fights Tagha on the temple and the rest of the Gaang fight the Denied (who are instant Airbending experts) below. At some point Tagha connects the staff to the temple and becomes a big blue monster, and they fight some more, and then Aaang connects the staff to the temple and he becomes a big blue monster, and almost blasts Tagha with the staff4 but resists and destroys the staff instead.

The Denied lose all their powers, and Tagha and the whole temple break up into shiny blue dust and crumble away. Later Aang and Katara open an Air Temple in Republic City and find a flock of sky bison,

My review

I’ll start with the good. The art is beautiful, and the new character designs are pretty good evolutions of the original. You can thirst after Zuko again and it’s not creepy anymore. Aang’s easy on the eyes himself. There are some extremely cute sky bison at the very end. That’s about where the good stuff ends.

First of all, this movie spends an ungodly amount of time — like half the runtime — on indulgent nostalgia porn. It opens with a long dream sequence of kid-Aang hanging out with Monk Gyasto. There’s a long intro sequence narrated by adult Aang where we see all the kid people doing bending moves turning into their adult selves doing bending moves, and Aang tells us about how great all his friends are and how they ended the war together. Each member of the Gaang gets a multi-minute fanservice-y intro sequence of them doing their thing when Aang’s messenger bird finds them. Katara gives Tagha a lecture about how peaceful Aang is while Aang slowly bends each of the elements one by one to recover the staff. It feels like 15% of this movie is in slow motion.

Unfortunately, nostalgia porn was more or less the best this movie had to offer. All the new elements it introduces massively cheapen the carefully restrained worldbuilding of the original:

  • The Avatar world is not supposed to be the kind of place with random magical MacGuffins that “channel the full power of the Spirit world” and turn you into a big blue monster more powerful than an Avatar. The Spirit World is not a battery pack, it’s a place full of beings and it’s mysterious and remote! And also normal non-Avatars should not be able to jump into a water-fish and just go there!5

  • The bending has become completely ungrounded, nothing feels like it’s based on a specific martial arts tradition. Everything is energy beams and body slams. Tagha mostly makes air by twirling his fingers a bit.

  • Is Sonam really the one Avatar who messed up so uniquely badly that she alone is cut off from all future lives? And if she presided over a Golden Age of Air Nomads, no one had written records of that? Aang wasn’t taught about her?

  • Why was Tagha so overpowered? How did he know all this Airbending that the greatest masters of Aang’s time didn’t know anything about? Why is it that two Airbenders can fly together if one can’t fly on their own? (And why was that some big lost secret Aang didn’t know about?)

  • Apparently there’s a whole “Immortal Storm” going on in the Endless Ocean that no one had heard of? There were Air Nomads in Aang’s time, they didn’t fly there?

  • My man was in the Avatar state practically nonstop in this movie, it didn’t feel like he was channeling past lives or that he was in unique peril or even honestly uniquely powerful in that state.

  • Everyone was killed, and then Katara was automagically revived by spirit water, and then she singlehandedly brought back three ordinary mortals from the dead…offscreen?? Remember what an ordeal it was to nurse Aang back to health after Azula’s lightning strike?

But this movie's gravest sin is what it did to its characters. Aang rounds up the leaders of the free world to go on some fetch quest, and they just…go along with this? Zuko is a Lincoln figure holding the factions together in a fragile post-colonial Fire Nation.6 What was the plan if he died? The world could have been plunged into war again. It was shameful of Aang to call on him, and unforgivable of Zuko to show up without a second thought.

And why was Aang abandoning the citizens of the Republic to run off for days at a time collecting relics in the first place? He has a city to lead. Years ago, Avatar Yangchen had said to a twelve year old Aang, “Selfless duty calls for you to sacrifice your own spiritual needs, and do whatever it takes to protect the world.” He was willing to listen then, and the tradeoff is not so harsh now. If he’s so worried about the extinction of the Air Nomads, he could stay and govern, and I dunno, make some babies on the side.

The real Katara would not have let him get away with this bullshit. At the beginning, she gently tells him that Republic City needs him. When he almost gets them all killed, she’s angry about it for two seconds.

Aang should have been furious! This stranger knowingly sent his wife and best friends (again, the leaders of the free world) to their deaths. He should have gone into the Avatar state over this.7 Instead he accuses Katara of not understanding his pain and orders them to keep going, and she immediately backs down. He never apologizes, and she never brings it up.

In the original show, little Aang had many moments of selfish indulgence, of failure to grapple with stakes. But they were forgivable and even endearing parts of his journey. The original Avatar was a coming of age story — the story of a carefree kid who had spent his whole life running from responsibility, and eventually learned to shoulder great responsibility with a degree of grace. I wanted to see the story of a man who had grown in his responsibilities and the grace with which he shouldered them.

1

It actually opens with a gratuitous dream sequence of child Aang being whimsical with the other air kiddos and Monk Gyatso, as I discuss later.

2

Aang puts it back with some Avatar state action.

3

Toph wrenches it back together with some metalbending action.

4

The staff…gives people Airbending, right? It’s not a generic laser blaster. Right?

5

Korra had already cheapened the Spirit World a lot, but this movie makes that even worse.

6

Sokka and Toph, to be fair, didn’t seem to have quite such a high opportunity cost at this time. But why? Why is Sokka not in Republic city, why is he some loser wannabe inventor in the South Pole? We know he becomes a councilman, let’s see that! And Toph is just teaching some kids metalbending somewhere in the Earth Kingdom. We know she starts the police force, let’s see that in action! The whole Gaang should have been in Republic City other than Zuko. Would have cut down on the fanservice-y intros.

7

That should have been the one and only time.

item.title: The Gorgon
item.content:encoded:
The Gorgon looms behind you, shifting in the corner of your eye, casting its shadow over the world. You catch glimpses through mirrors. Sometimes you see a forked tongue reflected in a thin boy begging at a crowded intersection, or the flash of a scale reflected in a little white mouse twitching in the jaws of an alleycat.

But the Gorgon is vast, and these little mirrors so low to the ground only show you glimpses of the tips of individual hairs upon its head. If you are going to slay the Gorgon, you must try to build new mirrors, wide and strangely curved, mounted high up and far away.

---

You’re in the lunch line at a conference where you’re supposed to tempt the brightest minds to care more about doing research on improving the tools with which we can eventually slay the Gorgon. Lunch is chicken.

When you were young and skinny and self-righteous, you would have forced yourself to picture the crowds of overgrown birds limping along on broken limbs in a fetid warehouse and pecking at each other’s festering sores with stump breaks. Forced yourself to be Not Okay with it. You used to make a point of watching an undercover factory farm video every few months. You would rehearse the horror of it, indulge in it.

This did not seem to bring you any closer to slaying the Gorgon, so the habit shriveled like a vestigial organ. And it was never much fun either.

The brightest minds do not live always with the Gorgon looming over them, flickering in the corner of their eye, and they like their lean protein. You eat your cauliflower, unbothered, and make small talk.

---

You’re finishing up a retro on communication challenges that came up in the process of getting feedback on a draft report informing policymakers that they should consider implementing transparency requirements to put themselves in a better position to address future risks that could derail the course of civilization enough to prevent us from maturing to the point where we can fully slay the Gorgon.

You have built an apparatus of mirrors upon mirrors that bend and scatter and bounce the light into a broad and fuzzy image. Rarely do you glimpse the sharp fork of a serpent’s tongue these days.

Even through all the mirrors, some people perceive the Gorgon’s form clearly enough to be petrified. You heard Brian Tomasik moved to the middle of nowhere because the water system there didn’t maim as many invertebrates. You think this is cowardly and self-indulgent. But you envy his eyesight.

---

It’s noon on a Monday and you’re forty six messages deep in a Slack thread about the strategy for how conciliatory you should be in your draft response to an effortpost on the EA forum criticizing how your organization handled an HR issue. You think of the butterfly meme. Is this…saving the world? You go to lunch.

Around the lunch table, someone tells you about the game theory of when aliens would be incentivized to produce “optimized disvalue.” You do not shudder. He jokes about the odds that he could think a thought that gets him sent to Hell. You are distracted by lingering personnel issues on your ops team. The conversation drifts to the dolorium-to-hedonium ratio. You have to run to a meeting.

item.title: Til death or the Singularity
item.content:encoded:
My post about marriage escaped my little bubble, so I got a lot of confusion and scorn about this throwaway sentence:

Given AI timelines, I think the expected length of your marriage if you get married today is probably something like ten years.

Let me back up and explain.

Within seven or eight years, I think there will probably be millions or billions of AI agents that are each far better than the very best humans at every skill in every field: each one far better than Einstein or von Neumann at physics, far better than Bezos or Musk at running giant companies, far better than the best generals at running a war effort, far better than any human at coming up with brilliant and creative new ideas, running massive ambitious enterprises, adapting to new situations, and learning new skills. This vast population of superhuman AI agents will likely invent new technologies radically faster than humans could on our own, 1 including developing even more powerful successors. A year or two into this process, the fast-evolving AI civilization will likely develop truly sci-fi technologies like near-light-speed spacecraft or molecular nanotechnology.

This — dizzying acceleration of technological progress driven by ever-more powerful AI — is often called the Singularity. What does the Singularity mean for your life?

Firstly, it could make life very short. AI could make it trivial to develop extremely destructive technologies like mirror bacteria, a small group could monopolize the most capable AI and use it to take over the world, there could be an all-out war between the US and China over control of AI or fought with AI-enabled superweapons, or (as I study in my day job) AI systems themselves could take over the world. I think we live in an era more dangerous than the height of the Cold War. I’m thirty one, and I think there’s a one in six chance that I personally die because of AI before my fortieth birthday.

If it does not kill you, the Singularity would probably make your life much, much longer and much, much stranger. You could have access to technology that lets you completely arrest biological aging, arbitrarily modify your appearance, give yourself new senses and physical abilities, permanently increase your intelligence or alter your personality. You could upload your brain to the cloud, copy yourself millions of times, and surgically edit your own “code.” If you wanted, you could become something far more than human.

Predicting the future is hard. We may not develop superintelligent AI for a long time, or it could prove difficult for even superintelligent AI to develop such technologies, or humans could collectively decide to restrain technological progress to a more manageable pace. But ultimately, if we don’t die, I think we will probably have radical life options within a few years of superintelligence.

What does the Singularity mean for marriage? Some rationalists who expect to live extremely long lives vow to stay together “til the stars burn out.” I think it’s silly, and borderline meaningless, to make a commitment now that is meant to last potentially millions of years of growth. I also think it’s probably not advisable to make a firm commitment to stay together in the face of radical technological options which the institution of marriage wasn’t designed to give guidance about. What if one partner wants to upload themselves and the other doesn’t? How would they handle a decision about whether to fully specify their children’s genomes? What if, with the advice of an infinitely knowledgeable deity, one partner or another can become extremely confident that they would be much better off broken up? What if they could both date AI partners that are supernaturally perfect for them?

If you survive the Singularity, I think you should plan on taking a deep breath and figuring out what your new life should look like. Your marriage vows should probably be until death or the Singularity.2 If the Singularity is pretty soon, that means your marriage will be pretty short.

But a shorter marriage can still be an incredibly meaningful one. I expect each passing year to be more intense than the last from now until the end. I feel I am staring at a cresting wave miles high about to break on our shore, and I am grateful to have someone’s hand to hold as I face the tsunami. It feels like getting married before heading off to war.

1

As I mentioned in a post on my other blog, some people believe that AI will only serve as the next innovation that’s needed to keep progress chugging along at its previous pace, rather than slowing down (the “no takeoff” view). This misses the fact that previous technologies never actually removed the human bottleneck entirely.

2

You could go more hardcore than this if you talk through the possibilities in advance. For example, you could agree that you and your partner owe each other one subjective lifespan (e.g. fifty subjective years). This does have significant costs —if one partner wants to upload and the other doesn’t, the more radical partner is giving up a lot to stay as a normal human with the more conservative partner — but it could make sense for you. If you make this commitment, your marriage would be about as long if you live through the Singularity as if there were no Singularity. In expectation, it is still shorter because there’s a significant chance you die in the middle of the Singularity.

item.title: Giving from the heart
item.content:encoded:
On Wednesday, my husband and I made a donation to the American Meat Producers Association to oppose the Save Our Bacon Act, a rider to the Senate Farm Bill that would undo state animal welfare laws like California’s Prop 12, which bans the sale of gestation crate pork and other meat from animals kept in extreme confinement, and stop states from passing any new welfare laws. I also called my Senators to (in their case) thank them for their public opposition to the bill, and urge them to also reject a compromise that would preserve existing laws but preempt new ones.

You can see posts by Dwarkesh Patel and Bentham’s Bulldog1 for more context on SOB and what you can do if you want to help. There’s been heartening momentum — since we made our donation, one of the most entrenched supporters of the bill has withdrawn his support (those close to the situation think this was likely as a direct response to AMPA ads targeting him), and the Manifold Market on the SOB Act dropped from ~26% chance it would pass to ~14%.

I don’t look much at this vast dark part of the world these days. When we made the decision to give, I cried. I cried at the thought of billions of animals living in pain and darkness from birth to death. And I cried at the immense, almost grotesque, power that we had to bestow grace on these creatures with the click of a button. Power we almost never choose to exercise.

I have complicated feelings about this donation. The whole deal with EA is that you’re supposed to try to have as much impact as you can with your resources, and according to my views, helping to save the country’s animal welfare laws was extremely unlikely to be the highest impact use of that money. I expect that superintelligent AI will likely be unleashed on the world in a matter of years, and this will determine the entire course of civilization from here on out. Ensuring that this monumental transition doesn’t end in disaster, and shaping it for the better, is by far the most important priority right now.

But I hate factory farming. I hate the callousness and venality of those on the other side of this battle. In an hour of urgent need, as the troops were being rallied, I hated the idea of looking these animals in the eye and saying I wouldn’t join their fight because we had to invest everything now so we could have as much money as possible to run AI agents doing technical safety experiments during crunch time, or bid on galaxies after the Singularity.

It was not the highest impact thing we could have spent that money on, but this fight truly moved me to give. I haven’t experienced that in a long while, and I hope to hold onto it.

When I was twenty, I led a gaggle of other college students to take the Giving What We Can Pledge to give 10% of our annual income to the most effective charities.2 While I’m pretty sure I’ve given away more than 10% of my total income over the last eleven years, I honestly haven’t tracked it very systematically.

At the time that I took the Pledge, I assumed (per the standard EA career advice at the time) that I would earn to give as a software engineer or trader after I graduated. Instead, I ended up graduating early to join Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving).

Very quickly, it became clear that I had influence over orders of magnitude more money than I could give myself. And my work was mentally exhausting.3 Personal giving decisions, which I envisioned being an intellectually and spiritually invigorating change of pace from a standard corporate job, became an awkward afterthought. The opportunities I understood best were very well funded (at least according to me), and I wasn’t really jazzed about tossing in another $15K on top of a $2.4M grant we’d just deliberated over.4 For several years I just entered the donor lottery, and thankfully lost every time.

I no longer work for the largest funder of all the causes I care about,5 though my husband and I do have substantially more to give than I would on my own. And these days, with increasingly compressed AI timelines and a huge amount of new money about to enter the space and political fundraising operations ramping up ahead of what will probably be the highest-spending and highest-stakes midterm and general election in US history, there’s now more energy around individual giving than there has ever been since the very early days of EA and the idea of earning to give. A big part of my impetus for giving to this now was the sense of running out of time to do anything good with the money, a worry that we would just go to our grave with it.

I don’t fully endorse this impulse,6 but there is something in it that I want to honor. My day job is still my top priority, but I don’t want to completely neglect the intellectual, pragmatic, and spiritual question of how best to direct the money my husband and I are stewarding in accordance with our shared values (and I don’t want to die with it). With this blog, I’ve managed to carve out an activity deeply connected to my values, that I systematically invest in, that isn’t just my day job. I hope to get there with our giving too.

1

Note that Bentham’s post says that the donations are many times more cost-effective than the next best animal welfare intervention, but at least at the point we donated I don’t think that was really true; it was perhaps ~30-50% better than the next best farm animal welfare opportunity according to advisors I trust who are following the situation closely. I think the discrepancy is both because we gave at a later time (when the cost-effectiveness had fallen) and because my sources likely had smaller estimates to begin with than Bentham’s sources.

2

At the time I took the pledge, I think it was technically about cost-effectively helping the poorest people in the world; it was later broadened.

3

We tracked our time using Toggl, and I tried to be scrupulous about it, pausing the timer when I went to the bathroom or answered a text message. I was devastated to learn that I only actually tracked hours in the very low 30s this way, even though it felt to me like I was pushing myself really hard and had no slack to do anything complicated outside of work.

4

Many of these organizations were also run by my friends, and allocating all my personal giving to slightly increase my friend’s salary felt like a kind of lame self-dealing.

5

The effect of this is more psychological than practical; I could still have a lot of influence over cG’s giving, as well as the giving of other individuals and institutions who collectively have a lot more to give than me and my husband, if I put effort into this.

6

In fact, the very next day after we made this donation, I found myself in a conversation full of longtermist EAs worrying that all the newly minted billionaires would quickly spend down their money on global health and animal well-being interventions instead of saving it for more removed but ultimately higher-leverage opportunities that crop up during (or even after) the Singularity.

item.title: Loosening the grip of utilitarianism
item.content:encoded:
Intellectually, I’m a moral anti-realist; the position that claims about right and wrong are the same type of object as claims about tables and chairs seems untenable. But in practice, my moral thinking has a realist flavor. I don’t ask myself what I care about or what matters to me, I ask myself what I “should” care about or what “actually” matters, and mostly shove aside the uncomfortable lack of grounding for what “should” or “actually” means.

I’ve also long held a cynical view of my own mind, in which most of my intuitions and desires are fundamentally irrational, and obstacles to achieving my goals. I strived to always do the prudent and logical thing whether or not it felt good. Do all your homework instead of staying out with your friends, date the stick-in-the-mud straight-A student instead of the hot stoner kid, major in computer science instead of creative writing.1

I brought this same dour tiger mom energy to moral deliberation. My working model was that moral questions have an obvious logical answer, and that obvious conclusion would often be unappealing because I’m selfish and irrational and weak. Moral evolution thus consisted primarily in having the grit to accept the obviously correct answer despite my irrational biases and do the obviously good thing despite my self-serving impulses.

Naturally, I latched onto utilitarianism, which was both maximally selfless and maximally logical. At first it was the drowning child argument, which felt to me like a commandment from God. But the utilitarian logic quickly drove me (as it did so many young EAs) to change my focus from global poverty to animal welfare, and then from animals to the far future.

Both shifts were an application of moral grit. I intuitively cared more about humans than animals, but the force of the utilitarian logic compelled me to abandon the bed nets and cash transfers. The arguments for obsessive focus on the far future were a bit tougher, but I chewed through a few long dry books on population ethics and was forced to conclude that creating a new person was morally equivalent to saving a life, and thus that preserving the long-term future had to be 10^big times more important than helping any number of beings in the present.

In both cases, I was deeply emotionally conflicted, and much more emotionally attached to the cause area I had abandoned. But that was the way it was supposed to be. The whole game was about having the discipline to act on values that are more impartial and selfless than what I actually felt, and utilitarian calculus was the tool that imposed this discipline. Like an arranged marriage, it was only after working on the cause that looked good on paper for a while that I started to feel some love for it.

In reading all those population ethics books over the course of making the painful switch to long-termism, I engaged with the many “repugnant conclusions” of utilitarianism. Indeed I did find them repugnant, which was a big part of why I resisted the perspective.

Here’s an omnibus ultra-repugnant conclusion that hits a lot of beats at once. There is a hell containing a trillion innocent people suffering horribly. You have the resources to rescue all of these beings and give them rich and amazing lives filled with love and joy. Or you could use those same resources to buy a lottery ticket with the following payout:

  • 999,999,999,999 in a trillion chance of tremendously increasing the suffering experienced by everyone in that hell.

  • 1 in a trillion chance of creating N short-lived copies of Hitler feeling one second of slight satisfaction at the fact that those people are suffering so much.

Classical utilitarianism dictates, of course, that there is some N for which you are morally obligated to buy the lottery ticket. There is no act-omission distinction, there are no individual rights, a massive population of rich joyful lives can be outweighed by a big enough pile of the barest pleasure, sadistic pleasure is just as good as any other, diversity of experience doesn’t matter, and you have to accept a near-certainty of arbitrary downside for the infinitesimal chance of a big enough gain.

But ultimately, this felt like another case where I simply had to apply moral grit. Of course my irrational intuition said to rescue all those suffering people instead of doing the weird sadist lottery thing. But that was just because I was irrationally scope-insensitive and had various aesthetic biases toward “narratively satisfying lives” or “virtuous joy” or “human rights” or whatever. There was nothing deep or interesting to be gained by patiently exploring my emotional resistance; I had to suck it up and eat bullets for breakfast every day until they started to taste okay.

I fully made the switch to long-termism in 2017. Ironically, 2017 was also when I hit Peak Utilitarianism. Since then, my moral views have gradually grown much more complicated and confused. I haven’t identified as a utilitarian in several years, despite the fact that utilitarianish thinking continues to be the main distinguishing feature of my ethical approach. The hardcore utilitarian kids I grew up with seem to have gone through a similar journey, and I believe few of them would now straightforwardly identify as a utilitarian. In fact, somewhere along the way I realized that the wise elders who had thought hardest about the intricacies of moral philosophy had never really been utilitarians in the first place.

There’s obviously a huge amount to say about this. I’ve tried several times to write out a substantive account of my shifts over the years,2 but the task is intimidating.

One piece of the shift is that I journeyed into stranger philosophical terrain and came back thinking that the dream of a straightforward bullet-biting utilitarianism was probably incoherent, or at the very least would need to be transformed into something new, something whose contours I couldn’t fully see.3 But actually working through all these gnarly philosophical questions to my satisfaction never seemed like the highest-impact activity,4 so all I have is a tangle of questions and confusions and half-remembered arguments. This does not constitute a comprehensive rebuttal to a committed utilitarian, let alone a coherent alternative view.5

But these questions and confusions were enough to loosen the intellectual grip utilitarianism held on me. This gave me the breathing room to go back to the drawing board, and consider whether I wanted to fully embrace moral intuitions I had previously chosen to subordinate to utility. And the idea of honor bubbled up.

At face value, utilitarianism seems to recommend acting dishonorably in a wide variety of normal situations: lying about how counterfactual a donation match is to get people to give more to your favored charity, or fudging your resume to make it more likely you’re hired for an important policy role, or using shoddy “scary demos” to scare policymakers about AI for reasons you don’t believe in yourself, or any number of other shady tactics.

I always felt averse to this. The same voice that tells me to alleviate others’ suffering (and brought me to EA) also tells me to be honorable — to tell the truth, deal fairly with people, keep my promises, follow the rules.

While I felt like I had to be a utilitarian, I told myself being honorable was actually perfectly compatible with utilitarianism: if you’re shady, people will lose trust in you, which will limit your ability to have more impact in the long run. But this is some weak tea,6 and it was clearly not my true rejection. If the negative consequences were really my only reason for wanting to be honest and cooperative, then I would have thought about the consequences for more than ten seconds.

Ultimately, I think I just care deeply about being an honorable person. I also care deeply about having a large altruistic impact. These are not usually in a massive amount of tension with one another; I’m fortunate to have a job where I can make a difference to one of the world’s most pressing problems by trying to understand the truth and share that with the world. But there are probably ways I could increase my impact by being more ruthless. In practice, I am trading some utility for honor. And that means that whatever I am, I am not quite a utilitarian.

1

This is an attitude I associate with LessWrong and online rationalism from 15 years ago (which I strongly vibed with then) and anti-associate with CFAR and the in-person rationalist community since 2017 or so, which seems to pay a lot of attention to respecting and reconciling with one’s intuitions rather than impatiently overruling them.

2

For this blog post, I’ve cannibalized some language from an abandoned attempt from 2021 and an abandoned attempt from 2024; both have large unfinished sections.

3

The simplest component of this is that, AFAICT, infinities seem to break a total utilitarian’s ability to say that any action is better than any other action. That is, in an infinite universe, I believe the total utilitarian would find it completely indeterminate whether accelerating tech progress is more or less valuable than reducing x-risk, no matter how high you set the probability of x-risk to be, for Hillbert’s Hotel-style reasons. And “prioritize x-risk” was supposed to be the headline result to fall out of this whole moral exercise!

Utilitarians often retort that “infinity breaks everything anyway,” but at first blush it doesn’t seem to nearly as obviously break non-consequentialist ethical systems, and I haven’t seen good discussion of that from the hardcore utilitarians. You can also try to rescue the infinite ethics problem by enforcing a weighting system that makes everything add up to 1, like UDASSA, but most self-declared utilitarians don’t seem to care much about working out the implications of this view, and it seems to give up on the radical equality and impartiality that was the big selling point of utilitarianism in the first place.

Separately, I suspect — though haven’t fully worked out — that the simple classical utilitarian vision I had in my head at 22 would be fundamentally altered if I fully incorporated considerations like the Simulation argument (and what the Simulators might want from you), decision theories in which you can control the past or control what happens in causally-distant parts of the multiverse, evidential cooperation in large worlds, and other trippy ideas along these lines.

4

I deeply admire how my former colleague Joe Carlsmith found so much energy and time to work out this stuff for himself in his spare time, even as we were both working on giant reports for work. That didn’t feel accessible to me. It was hard to approach these big questions from a place of curiosity and patience and reflectiveness; I felt only urgency and frustration. This blog was inspired in part by Joe’s, but as you can see my posts are much shorter and I haven’t been able to cover nearly as much philosophical ground.

5

For years, I’ve dreamed of working through all these questions and writing up an epic blog post series about just how salvageable the simple utilitarian project is, but of course I’m kidding myself if I think I’ll get to this before the Singularity.

6

Unfortunately, a lot of people seem to have a lot of policy influence through blatant lies, propaganda, and smear campaigns.

item.title: The science of duty
item.content:encoded:
In everyday ethics, the right thing to do in a given situation depends on the particular social role you are playing in that specific context.

If you are a Catholic priest, and one of your parishioners reveals his intent to murder his wife in the context of sacramental confession, the rules of the Church obligate you not to call the police or warn his wife (or indeed reveal any indirect hint of your knowledge to anyone). If some dude at a bar tells you he plans to kill his wife, you are perhaps obligated to call the police. If your parishioner comes to your home in the middle of the night desperate for your counsel, the responsibilities of your role as a citizen and your role as this man’s priest are in tension, and the right course of action is fraught.

If you are someone’s defense attorney, you are obligated to vigorously raise as much doubt about the prosecution’s case as you can, even if you know he did it.1 If you are a juror listening to the arguments of the case, you are obligated to consider whether the prosecution’s case is established beyond a reasonable doubt, doing your best to ignore impermissible kinds of evidence. If you are the judge, and the jury has only found the defendant guilty of manslaughter, you must not choose an extraordinarily harsh sentence merely because you strongly suspect he actually committed murder.

After Biden’s disastrous debate with Trump sparked calls for him to step down, Matt Yglesias (a Democrat) said something I found striking:2

Columnists calling on Biden to step down provide…a small boost to Trump’s election odds and a minuscule increase in the odds that Biden actually steps aside. I think we have to say it anyway, because this is journalism and we owe a duty of truth to our audience. But in narrow cost-benefit terms, the public criticism of Biden has negative expected value.

Elected officials have a different set of responsibilities. I’ve seen some people express frustration that Barack Obama came out with such a strong statement of support for Biden. But Obama slagging Biden in public would have been a boon to Trump and accomplished nothing. Same for Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries and Nancy Pelosi and everyone else who matters. These are politicians, and they do not share journalists’ obligations of candor.

In these cases, the ethical responsibilities associated with your social role call on you to explicitly disavow heroic responsibility for outcomes. As a journalist, it is not your job to ensure that the candidate you believe would be best for the country gets into power; that is the job of the citizens as they cast their vote. As a lawyer or juror or judge, it is not your job to see to it that murderers are stopped no matter what; that is the job of the legal system — a machine made out of human cogs, one of which is you.

This mental move of not doing everything in your power to achieve the Good, of willingly surrendering your agency over the fate of the world to systems outside yourself, is unnatural in a utilitarian framework. Most3 self-described utilitarians do make some concession to “deontological constraints” in practice, whether because abiding by such constraints is supposedly instrumentally useful4 or because something something moral uncertainty. But seeing deontology (literally “the science of duty”) as primarily being in the business of imposing “constraints” is itself a very consequentialist lens on the whole endeavor.

In fact, the responsibilities associated with various social roles frequently call on you to take active, positive actions that may conflict with utility. As a defense attorney, you are called on to throw all your mental faculties into making the most vigorous defense of your client that you can; it is ethically suspect to do less than that because you think he probably belongs behind bars. As a journalist, Matt felt called by a duty of candor to loudly voice an opinion that he thought would hurt his favored political party, the country, and the world. As a participant in intellectual discourse, I believe you are often called on to volunteer weak points in your arguments and the best case against your most important beliefs.

But isn’t all this business with roles and responsibilities simply instrumental to utility? On some level, yes (though not the utilitarian’s notion of impartial global utility). The legal and social roles we have in our modern society, and our rich understanding of what it means to perform the duties of these various roles, emerged because they helped people live together more harmoniously, which allowed people to broadly get more of what they wanted.

If this explains our deontological ethical intuitions, does it explain them away? Understanding our deontological intuitions as a set of cognitive tools to help us get along in a society does not automatically tell us whether to embrace or reject deontology — any more than understanding our empathy for the vulnerable as an extension of parental instincts can tell us whether to embrace or reject utilitarianism.

Since I hit Peak Utilitarianism, the concepts of roles and responsibilities have worked their way closer to being first class citizens in my own moral parliament. It’s totally possible for a self-described utilitarian to get to a functionally similar place by layering on some epicycles, or going through a long detour involving decision theory. But sometimes it’s nice to think in the language my brain was built to understand.

1

Although you are also obligated not to knowingly lie to the court in the course of this defense.

2

I am not actually sure I agree with Matt that the journalists calling on Biden to step down were net negative for the cause of beating Trump; my best guess is they were helpful. But the important thing here is that Matt believed this would be net negative on consequentialist grounds when he wrote this. (If I am right that these efforts were positive for the relevant cause, then Matt’s behavior may be a case of, as Scott Alexander suggests, “simple virtue” being “self-righting, like a Daruma doll - stable against a failure in forecasts.”

3

Though not all

4

As I discussed last time, I am unconvinced that the pragmatic argument (”abiding by deontological constraints is actually what’s best for long run utility after all”) actually goes through, certainly not enough to recover the full spectrum of deontological intuitions that I’d like to preserve.

item.title: I'm never satisfied
item.description: But we get the job done
item.content:encoded:
I was twenty one when I joined Open Phil,1 as a zealous young EA who had idolized the organization since I was in high school (back when it was called GiveWell Labs). I worked there for over nine years, leaving about six months ago (shortly after it rebranded as Coefficient Giving). By the time I left, I was kind of a fixture in the organization, and a significant driver of culture and thought within the AI team of 45-ish people. My manager felt that a lot of people on the team would be worried to see me go, and encouraged me to convey that I believed in their work in my goodbye message.

If you read that message, I meant what I said. I do think the kind of ambitious, foresightful philanthropy that OP (ugh fine, cG) does at its best is extremely impactful, and I do think the AI team is really great and has unique strengths.

But before I articulated that, I sat at my desk for over an hour, holding back tears, struggling to compose something not totally deranged. The first goodbye draft that leapt to mind was along the lines of: “I’m leaving because I failed to figure out how to add value here for years and years and years, even though I had every opportunity and everyone else around me managed to figure it out, and whatever defects were responsible for that will probably also cause me to fail wherever I go next, but I know for sure I’ll keep failing if I stay, so I guess I have to at least try leaving on the off chance that I manage to succeed at something somewhere.”

Let me back up. For the last decade, my work has followed a bipolar rhythm. I’ll latch onto some grand vision for The Highest Impact Thing to Do and throw myself into executing on it, only to realize 6-18 months in I’m only ever going to be capable of achieving a small fraction of the grand dream and the theory of change has big holes in it and other interventions are probably higher impact actually. Then I’ll spend 2-4 months hating myself and everything I’ve ever done and casting desperately for the Actually Impactful Thing to Do until I build up a head full of steam about another vision and start all over.

I have done several rounds of this, from EA community building to researching the stuff Open Phil told me to research to running a brutal yet productive hiring round to insane philosophy to slightly less insane timelines forecasting to business operations to alignment agendas and threat modeling to funding to “advising” to finally risk assessment at METR, and have written countless dozens of other vision docs in periods of desperate searching that never budded into projects. Despite staying in one place for almost a decade, I never built something that lasted even two years. I hired many great people into cG but I never managed them for very long. Over and over, it just felt like I’d made the wrong bet, had the wrong vision; over and over, I lost faith before I doubled down. Two rounds ago it got bad enough that I took a four month leave of absence just to figure out my shit (I didn’t).

I’m aware that deep shame and dissatisfaction about your work is rooted in pride, a sense that you should be able to do so much more. And as my long-suffering husband repeatedly points out, all this shame and paranoia is wasted motion. Maybe if I strung more than two and a half thoughts together in series without freaking out that I’m wrong to work on what I’m working on right now or I’m spending too much time thinking about what to work on next or I don’t stick with things long enough or I don’t explore widely enough or I’m too biased to think about any of this the right way, I’d have the mental energy to figure out better things to do and execute on them better. I have no great reply to this. But in some core part of myself, I know — no matter what logical arguments I nod along to — I know that this paranoia is what separates me from the beasts.

I’ve often compared myself to the anxious romantic who bounces from one perfectly functional relationship to the next, overthinking and sabotaging each one in turn because they don’t feel The Spark anymore or they’re not 100% sure he’s The One. I’m blessed with an immigrant’s steely pragmatism in the romance department,2 and if it weren’t for my experiences with trying to decide what I should be doing, I would have less pity for those who tie themselves in knots over love.

When I left cG, a small part of me harbored a quiet hope that these old psychological strictures would suddenly burn away and a new me would rise from the ashes. Alas, I remained frustratingly myself.

But I did get something in my new role that I’d never had before: a tight-knit team working on the same thing with me. The inside of my own mind remained a bit of a suffocating and cacophonous place, but I didn’t have to spend nearly as much time in there. Most importantly, in the period where the writing was most intense, my primary coauthor was always there, day or night or weekend. In all my previous writing projects I’d fought alone through daily waves of doubt and despair for endless weeks or months. In this one, the same moments of potential despair would crop up but then the right way to articulate this crucial point or the best strategy to sidestep that conceptual minefield or the approach for rescuing some partially-right argument would kind of just tumble out of us in conversation. For large chunks, we sat side by side writing every word together. I had never realized working could be so easy.

Leaving cG didn’t break the cycle. I am currently in the phase where I desperately re-examine whether the thing I did actually didn’t make sense3 and I should be doing something totally different that Actually Has Impact, as I was when I was trying to compose that goodbye message in December. I feel like we are entering the AI mid-game — everything is picking up, and the gameboard keeps shifting. No plan seems like it comes close to matching the enormity of the challenge, and I feel like we collectively only have a couple more swings to take before it’s all over, and we need to make them count. I don’t know what the best thing to do is, and I don’t know exactly what I’ll do next. But I’m tremendously grateful that this time, I don’t need to figure that out all by myself.

1

I interned there the summer after my sophomore year of college, and the following year I graduated early to join full time, starting in July 2016.

2

I was going to write about how people should think about dating more like they’re arranging their own marriage, but fellow brown girl and rat Aria Schrecker has already written approximately infinity posts about this for me.

3

Who exactly is the audience for this kind of report, and what are they supposed to do differently? Is that going to be enough? Is it going to come in time? What other products could we produce instead with our currently extremely scarce analytical capacity?

item.title: Making meaning better
item.content:encoded:
To live a fulfilling life, most humans need to feel conviction that they are a part of, and contributing to, something bigger than themselves. Historically, we’d derive this feeling through activities like making shoes or bread or fishing rods or other goods that those around us found useful, adhering to elaborate rules of diet or dress or speech in obeisance to gods and traditions, and raising children to learn our trades and honor our gods and carry on our traditions.

Somewhat infamously, modern atomized godless capitalist etc society has made it harder to access these traditional paths to purpose and meaning.1 It’s harder to feel conviction that we are useful to other people, because labor is divided so finely that we can’t intuitively grasp its value: a random admin worker in a mature market economy may in fact provide more practical benefit to other humans than the local carpenter in a village 700 years ago,2 but their impact is distributed across millions of people they won’t ever meet and blends chaotically with millions of other micro-impacts from different strangers. It’s harder to feel conviction in our religious practices, because of the thing where we realized religion isn’t actually true.3 We are still hardwired to enjoy our kids, but it’s harder to feel conviction in starting a family when it’s no longer the life path dictated by religion and tradition.4

I never really got to experience the normal modern ennui, or grapple with the challenge of creating one’s own meaning in a fundamentally meaningless universe in its classic existentialist form. I short-circuited all that when I found EA in high school.

I immediately oriented to the EA canon as pretty much the literal word of God. Part of the gospel was that the point of all this was emphatically not to derive a sense of purpose in life from the practice of EA, but to actually do the best thing, whatever it was and however you felt about it.5 But in making this point, early EA evangelists often chose safe punching bags — causes like giving to the opera, or Harvard, or the hypothetical Center for Curing Rare Diseases in Cute Puppies, that their audience would not find particularly meaningful. Meanwhile, the idea that I could save multiple babies every year just by donating a modest amount of the income I could expect to make felt astoundingly meaningful to me. I completely reshaped my life around it.

But over time, I’ve come to derive much less emotional meaning from my practice of EA, even as I increased my actual impact a lot.6 It turned out that there’s no simple formula to morality, the most important cause area is extremely abstruse and riddled with fundamental question marks, and most paths to impact probably won’t work and many could easily cause massive harm. And as I learned more and increased my discernment, I came to have significant reservations about pretty much every organization and leader that I would have previously followed energetically and unquestioningly.

And all of this also just…became more of an actual job. My brain is filled not with awe at the importance of the mission and gratitude at being in a position to contribute to it, but preoccupied by emails and office politics and project management. This is as it should be; the point is to do my job well, and stressing about a million details is the bread and butter of doing any job well.

I continue to believe that providing me with a sense of purpose is not the point of my work, and I haven’t stopped doing it.7 But in the early days of my EA journey, I had this youthful arrogance that the whole idea of people “needing” to feel a sense of “purpose” or “meaning” was bullshit, that I didn’t care about any of that or indeed understand what it even was. I now think this may have been a bit like a fish loudly announcing that it didn’t believe in water. If anything, I probably crave these things far more than the typical person8 — after all, that confession scene from Fleabag was one of the most relatable (and hottest) three minutes of TV in the last decade.

I've been trying to listen more to this need. I've carved out more space for nurturing sources of meaning that don't route through my day job: writing here on Good Bones, participating in more music and ritual in groups, doing beautiful things for my friends and community. But my journey very much feels incomplete. I would like to do for all this Singularity stuff what Carl Sagan did for the scientific materialist understanding of the universe, or what Milton Friedman (and Adam Smith) tried to do for the global market economy. As I build my skill at meaning-making, I hope to close the loop, and ground the actual work I do for the sake of impact in a deeper sense of purpose.

1

Honestly, we have very little evidence about how purposeful or meaningful people’s lives felt in the distant past, and there’s always a temptation to view the past through rose-colored glasses. Many of our ancestors’ lives were probably spiritually bleak in addition to (and because of) being materially deprived, dangerous, and unfree. However, other things being equal, I do believe there is something to the dynamic I’m describing — I’d bet there’s some set of emotional needs it’s harder to fulfill if you have a more secular worldview, more personal choice, weaker life scripts, and more transactional and impersonal relationships.

2

They are very likely adding much more value denominated in dollars, but of course the people these dollars flow to are much richer (and thus stand to benefit much less from marginal consumption) than Medieval peasants.

3

Some takeslingers want us to respond to the modern crisis of meaning by converting to Catholicism so we can RETVRN to a Godly life, but it’s just much less satisfying to try to live by God’s word when you understand in the back of your mind that you made up God so you could have Someone’s word to live by.

4

And comes at the expense of much more entertaining leisure options than our ancestors had.

5

This from Something to Protect has always stuck with me: “Similarly, in Western real life, unhappy people are told that they need a “purpose in life”, so they should pick out an altruistic cause that goes well with their personality, like picking out nice living-room drapes, and this will brighten up their days by adding some color, like nice living-room drapes. You should be careful not to pick something too expensive, though.”

6

Padme: Positive impact, right?

7

Though I did take a few months off in the fall of 2024, in significant part because I had somewhat exhausted my “meaning tank” and had to refill it.

8

Holding comfort and safety roughly equal, it’s plausible that I would have been much happier if I had been raised in some intense religious community that told me exactly what I needed to do to follow the will of God, and I could find no fault in their worldview. I wouldn’t want that, because I want to actually help people and have contact with reality. Also, realistically, such a religious community would have been poor and brutish and it would overall be bad.

item.title: So your girlfriend is sad
item.content:encoded:
I have what you might call “resting sad brain.” Whenever I’m not actively working on something or reading something or watching something or chatting with someone, my thoughts reliably drift toward painful things.

When I’m in a noble headspace, I ruminate over all the ways the Situation is terrifying, all the ways Society is reacting to it inadequately, all the ways We (me, my organization, my community) are bad and failing to do as much as we should. In pettier moods, I ruminate over minor and often one-sided conflicts with people who frustrate me. Really, I’m just walking around with a nameless pit in my stomach; when I’m paying attention, I can practically feel my brain filling in one post-hoc explanation or another.

Sad girls like me abound (especially, in my experience, in EA). Like my husband, you too might have been unwittingly snookered into falling in love with a smart, put-together lady only to find out she’s super sad all the time and you don’t get it.1 Don’t panic!

And that’s basically my advice: don’t panic. Years ago, on Caroline Ellison’s now-defunct tumblr, I ran across her review of tips from some odious late-aughts pickup artist for how to deal with women in relationships. I don’t remember most of them now, but what stuck with her stuck with me: think of yourself as an oak tree.

An oak tree weathers the thunderstorm, neither bending at its onslaught nor battling it. I think this is the foundation of handling it well when your girlfriend is sad. It is not about you.2 And it is not a problem.3 There is nothing for you to solve. It simply is, and you can handle it.

I think being okay must come before understanding and empathy. Yes, feeling understood is a deep emotional need. But let’s face it, you probably don’t understand this part of her very well right now, and you can’t begin to understand her better without feeling okay enough to muster curiosity and patience. And reflexive empathy can easily be misapplied — my husband sometimes gets into a trap where he’s torn between feeling absolutely horrible for me (because if he ever cried as hard as I was crying it would be because his entire family just died a torturous death) and feeling frustrated at me (because I’m crying so much even though not even one person came close to dying what the fuck??).

You need not frantically judge each sentiment she is expressing as logical or irrational, proportionate or over-the-top; there is no decision you face right now for which you need those judgments.4 Try to experience her emotion as something more akin to a natural phenomenon; relax into the experience as if you just jumped into a cold pool. If you find that you resonate with something she’s expressing, it reminds you of something you have felt before, tell her; that’s a wonderful gift you can give her. If you find that nothing does resonate, then respect her alienness and hold onto your love.

1

And if you’re just starting out in the dating world, you should know: the girls are sadder than they look.

2

Unless it is about you. Helping you figure out whether it’s about you is mostly beyond the scope of this post, but here’s a basic tip: just ask, early on, with as much calmness and openness as you can muster, whether she’s upset about something you did and offer to talk about that if she is. Then believe her answer. If she’s routinely upset at you but plays dishonest games about it, consider breaking up with her and finding someone else.

3

Maybe over time you’ll come to think that you should really push your girlfriend to go on antidepressants, or try therapy; that could be helpful. Or maybe you’ll decide that you don’t want to deal with these recurring episodes of sadness and you want to break up with your girlfriend; that would be your prerogative. But you don’t need to figure any of that out while she’s in the middle of an episode of great sadness; it’s exactly the wrong time to excavate patterns and figure out solutions. If you later decide that it’s important to do something specific about it, bring it up proactively in a moment of calm.

4

Maybe looking at the pattern of how she reacts and relates to many different people and events over time, you’ll decide that you don’t really respect her approach to life. That would be a great reason to break up with her. You don’t need to make that decision now.

item.title: Norms for illegible sacrifices
item.description: How much should you hate your job?
item.content:encoded:
Structurally, the basic logic of effective altruism is quite demanding, bordering on totalizing. Yes, most EAs are naturally very high integrity people in their hearts (in some ways the opposite of ruthless consequentialists); this sociological fact, plus a dash of esoteric decision theory and a sprinkle of pragmatic instrumental reasoning, means that the EA memeplex ends up very strongly discouraging violating norms for the greater good. But by default, there isn’t much of a limit on what the ideology can ask you to give of yourself.

But a real world community consisting of a large diverse group of people, almost all of whom will ultimately place a lot of weight on their own comfort and happiness, cannot practically coordinate around maximal sacrifice as the norm.

When it comes to donations, the EA community has borrowed from centuries-old social technology and settled on tithing. When it comes to work hours, most EAs basically default to the prevailing norms in their surrounding culture, which where I’m from is somewhere between the standard 9-to-5 and an intense hedge fund.1 Diet is the most heterogeneous, but big-tent EA spaces seem to have settled on a norm of offering beef and fish but not chicken, eggs, and pork, which cause substantially more animal suffering per calorie.

Percent of income donated, number of hours worked, and to some extent diet have two properties that make it easy to build norms around them: it’s relatively clearly observable what exactly everyone is sacrificing,2 and the total feasible sacrifice anyone could make is bounded (you can’t give more than 100%, you can’t work more than 100ish hours per week, you can’t eat less than no animal products). This makes it a lot easier for a group of humans to settle on and enforce some ultimately arbitrary middle ground without slippery-sloping down to zero or purity-spiraling up to infinity.

But there are a lot of other forms of sacrifice that are a lot harder to govern with the social technology we have.

When I was burned out and took time off to find myself a couple years ago, I talked to several fellow EAs about how they approached their life. One friend told me that back when the Thing to Do was earn to give at a hedge fund, he decided he wouldn’t do it even if it was arguably higher impact because it would eat into his soul too much. Now, by this point I was already many years into this EA gig and very much thought of myself as an annoying ecumenical elder rather than a hot-headed youth — but still, I was a little scandalized. Like, are you allowed to do that? When it would be the highest impact job?!

In the abstract, it doesn’t make much sense to be scandalized by that but not scandalized by people taking any days off or spending any money on themselves. I think a big part of what was going on for me was something like: “Well if we allow this, where will it end?” You can’t have an EA community that just lets you take whatever job you think is best for your soul; that kinda defeats the point. I can’t easily draw a line on how much you’re allowed to factor in your soul’s integrity into the career selection process, so I want to protect the norm that it just doesn’t count.3

There are many types of sacrifices you can make in a career. You can work long hours or work for little pay, yes — but also, you can be on call to jump into action at unpredictable hours. You can work on deeply confidential projects you can’t commiserate or celebrate with your loved ones. You can work alone, on something no one else believes in. You can do work that requires you to hide your true beliefs. You can be on the hook for making a lot of politically-loaded choices that will never make anyone happy and always make you feel dirty.4 You can spend your time dealing with Kafka-esque bureaucracies. You can take swings that could blow up in your face publicly. You can work with people you don’t like or respect.

The equilibrium right now seems to be that people mostly leave each other alone about career choices and emit some sort of bland message like “Impact is important but personal fit matters too.”5 Ideally, the community would develop some case law about this.
