Sometimes you really do need to take one for the team and do a really unpleasant job that is really important, and sometimes you need to unclench and let your freak flag fly.6 I wish we had scripts and case law about these kinds of choices; they are the most important ones we make.

1

More than one intense young EA has told me that when they first got sucked up into the professional scene, they were surprised and disappointed at how little most people worked.

2

At least on a basic level — of course, some people will have better returns to consumption than others, some people will experience more pain per hour worked, some people care more about the pleasure of eating good food or have health issues that make it more painful to be vegan.

3

To some extent, pushing to keep it out will drive it underground — people will be more inclined to find motivated reasons why the job that best feeds their soul is actually secretly their highest impact option. That said, this dynamic probably doesn’t claw back all the value.

4

On another one of my sabbatical conversations, another friend told me: “One thing I’m grateful for is that I get to feel thoroughly proud of my job. Not all jobs worth doing have that property.”

5

Our difficulty coming up with norms about this is very tied up in our difficulty coming to consensus about what’s high impact, beyond very crude cause-area-level heuristics like “AI risk is bigger than bio risk.” One of my deepest wishes for the community is that we had made better intellectual progress on these questions (sometimes called “macrostrategy” though I hate that word a lot), and now I think we have very little time to do it well.

6

One important dynamic here is that people are more likely to do well at their jobs if they like them, but it’s easy to take this valid heuristic too far — the job where you’ll have the most impact is probably not the one you’ll enjoy most.

item.title: Does power corrupt?
item.content:encoded:
Different people in the EA ecosystem relate very differently to the life strategy of accumulating power so you can later wield it for good. This is not really my beat, and like many people I intuitively feel like it’s a bit icky and scary, and have the vague sense that somewhere along the path to power I’ll lose my way. But I’m really torn about how much credence I should lend to these intuitions.

To get one thing out of the way first: I think SBF is an extreme non-example of “power corrupts.” The man was the same hardcore double-or-nothing utilitarian sociopath both before and after acquiring his billions, and I’ll bet he’s the same now that he’s lost it all. Power changed him very little.

No, SBF exemplifies a different pattern: “the corrupt gain power.”1 If someone seems unusually hungry for power, they’re probably an unusually bad person from a common sense perspective. And the ranks of the ultra-powerful tend to be populated by people who really, really wanted it — who were willing to sacrifice not just norms and decency, but also their own comfort and happiness, for it.

But these two memes make nearly the opposite recommendation to a good person. If power corrupts, you should try to avoid it. If it’s just that the naturally-corrupt tend to gain power, you should actively try to accumulate power to make up for that. I tend to suspect the latter is actually the more robust pattern in the real world.

This doesn’t mean there aren’t paths to corruption. As you get more powerful, people around you will want things from you and want to stay in your good graces and this can screw up your epistemics. If you get used to a certain lifestyle, it can make it harder to make career choices that require you to give that up. And you may need to do harmful things to actually get and hold onto power,2 which you might not be able to make up for when the time comes.3

But also, it might just be…fine. There aren’t actually that many clear-cut examples of people we know tried to acquire power specifically to make the world better, and many of those people turned out to be…fine?4 Overall, I am grateful when people who broadly share my values slug it out in economic and political competition and win, and try not to be too precious about it.

1

I think only some of the connotations of “corrupt” fit in this case. SBF is evidently very willing to lie and cheat to get what he wants, and it’s fair to call that corruption. But a very important part of his danger comes from his sincerely held ideology.

2

In the AI x-risk scene, the most classic example is “contribute to accelerating The Singularity.”

3

Of course, whether or not you can later make up for the harm you cause on the way to accumulating power depends a lot on how much you're allowed to just do a basic utilitarian cost-benefit analysis. Despite not being a utilitarian and taking duties and norms seriously, I generally tend to think that you more or less can offset the harm you caused in the course of doing something that's not actually illegal or strongly norm-violating in our actual real society (e.g. eating meat, working at an AI company) by doing something else more beneficial later. Vibes-wise, this is a disagreement I seem to have with many rats, who want us all to act-as-if AI research is extremely norm-violating to make that more true.

4

Pretty much all famously-good people in history who got a lot of good stuff done, from MLK to Nelson Mandela to your favorite President, likely tried to acquire more power so they could do more good.

item.title: Six thoughts on work
item.description: Doing hard things with other people
item.content:encoded:
I’ve been working a lot in the last few weeks. I try very hard to write a little bit every night, and I have not managed that in recent days. But I made a resolution to publish a blog post every week in 2026, and dammit, this is not the week I’m going to break my streak.1 Here are six thoughts about what it is to work hard alongside others:

  1. Working long hours with someone on something difficult and important is a deeply intimate thing. It breaks down some of the norms of our individualistic culture.2 You can’t ignore each other. You are forced to feel pain from one another’s shortcomings. You tell each other things like, “You really do need to cancel your dinner plans and work late tonight” and “You really fucked that up.” When I coauthored a report with my now-husband, we got much more frustrated with each other than we normally do but I also felt closer to him than I normally do. I would love to work with him again.3

  2. I know it’s supposed to be healthy to have friends outside your insular workaholic subcommunity. But it is also a great privilege to get to witness your friends hard at work on something that deeply matters. It makes a person more three dimensional.

  3. If you haven’t actually worked with someone on something, it is very hard to know just how good they are at what they do, and the precise ways in which they are good at what they’re good at and bad at what they’re bad at. Heuristics like their organization and their title and their vague reputation and how smart they sound are all very lossy.

  4. There’s no good substitute for a real external constraint. There have been many periods in my life where I pushed and guilted myself to work more on nebulous and poorly-scoped research projects, fighting through psychic resistance to eke out a few more hours here and there. There are other times when work is simply wrenched out of me — when I simply must get back to this person today or give that talk tomorrow. This work can tire the body, but there is so much less resistance from the soul. Doing reps of this is great for building self-trust.

  5. Having less time for everything else makes me more deeply appreciate diminishing returns. The first twenty minutes of seeing my housemates or my husband is just so good.

  6. People usually express a lot of sympathy for you in periods of very high stress and very hard work, and it’s not undeserved. But the dirty little secret is that such stretches can also be very fun. Everything is funnier when you’re sleep deprived.

1

If you’re wondering why there isn’t a post every week on this blog, it’s because some of them are over at Planned Obsolescence.

2

To be clear, I’m mostly a pretty big fan of our individualistic culture.

3

I imagine that there’s a similar dimension of intimacy you unlock in a marriage from raising children together. There’s not much of a substitute for doing something with real stakes that you are both invested in and both responsible for.

item.title: Growth without the mindset
item.content:encoded:
I basically have a fixed mindset about my own aptitudes and personality traits. To some extent, I was raised with it: the many Telugu aphorisms my dad would repeat included “You can’t straighten a dog’s tail” and “The fox was jealous of the tiger so it branded stripes onto itself.”1 At Open Phil, where I grew up a second time, they did not tell you about your “growth areas” — they told you about your goddamn weaknesses.

Mostly though, I was born with it.2 The can-do positivity associated with “growth mindset” is fundamentally pretty alien to me, and I can’t help but feel like it’s a bit twee or cringe. Flattering my biases, the dramatic pop psychology claims about the benefits of growth mindset mostly crumbled in the replication crisis. But I do think there’s something to it.

By growth mindset, I mean a tendency to consciously and deliberately invest effort into addressing weaknesses, practicing skills, and learning new things. Some people are really into this. They’ll make Anki decks to memorize facts about AI trends, or hire a coach to improve their management skills, or work through exercises in physics textbooks.

I am not like that. I can’t remember the last time I read a nonfiction book. I have basically no inclination to hire a coach or therapist, and it’s not for a lack of issues. I pretty much only learn stuff that I have to learn to do my job:3

  • As part of writing an old report on when we might train a model as powerful as the human brain, I read up on the transformer architecture and empirical risk minimization theory and actor-critic policy gradients and efficient batch sizes and a number of other technical topics to understand what I believed and how I should construct my arguments.4 I never studied that stuff before, and never have since. Other projects led me to brief forays into hyper-specific corners of thermodynamics, statistics, economics, and ethology.

  • I spent years at Open Phil working on a range of nebulous research and writing projects like this, vaguely feeling like I should get experience with grantmaking at some point but never getting around to it. Eventually, I developed a bunch of takes about AI safety research directions, which led me to want to fund certain kinds of research, which led me to finally make my first grant. From there I quickly escalated to take on our technical safety portfolio for a couple years.

  • To this day, I haven’t properly fired up an AI agent and vibe coded something. Sure, I use models to help me edit tricky emails and review contracts and do a bit of desk research here and there for my reports, but…well, my job is largely sending tricky emails and negotiating contracts and writing long carefully-worded reports; AI agents aren’t amazing at this. I have some dim sense in the back of my mind that whole new vistas of possibility should somehow be opening up, but I am never inspired to do anything.5

I do think I’m leaving value on the table because it’s so unnatural for me to adopt a growth mindset. I recently found myself investigating a misalignment incident, and my skillset meant that I worked almost entirely on writing. If at some point in the past I had sat down and decided to invest in developing my ML research skills, I would have been more useful in that project. I could have become decent at it if it was crucial for my job, but it never was so I never did.6

Still, you grow whether or not you have a growth mindset. I’ve certainly grown a lot in the last decade. Yes, I very rarely put deliberate practice into working on my weaknesses — in fact, I tried to select projects that would be loaded on my strengths and forgiving of my weaknesses. But this work was still challenging, and forced me to push even harder in the areas where I was already strong. As a result, I have become more and more extremely myself with each passing year.7 As an approach to work and life, this has a fair amount to recommend it.

1

At one point as a kid, I was sad that I wasn’t very good at music. My dad told me that when he was a kid he was sad that he couldn’t sing well and his big sister was like, “It’s okay, the world needs people to appreciate good singers too.” I soon gave up on music lessons and to this day am not particularly musical.

2

When I first learned about Calvinism in AP Euro my sophomore year of high school, I was entranced by how right it felt in my bones. God decides when you are born whether you go to Heaven or Hell, and nothing you can do will ever change that. But those predestined for Heaven work piously their whole life anyway, because that is simply who they are.

3

When my job was to be a student, I was a great student — I was genuinely moved by the beauty of the subject matter and formed a deep understanding of it. When I got a real job, I pretty much never thought about any of that again.

4

I now think that I was overly thorough in how I approached that project, and if I were doing it again I would find elegant ways to sidestep the reasons I felt like I needed to nail down all the stuff in order to write it.

5

Just like I never set up the elaborate cool-kid keyboard shortcuts that make typing more efficient.

6

At one point when I was burned out I made the uncharacteristic move of attending an ML / AI safety boot camp on the vague hope that I could transition to more technical work, and took away very little from it.

7

This can lead you to double- and triple-down on very niche superpowers. For example, one of my main skills is talking to very smart and slightly crazy guys with intriguing and very big-if-true ideas, and translating the actually good ideas into impact by explaining them clearly. There are many sub-skills to this skill, including the taste for who has good things to say, the conceptual vocabulary to understand what the hell they’re talking about, a nose for when something won’t quite hold up, the social presence and courage to push on it, the taste for how to modify it into something that is a bit more right, the particular writing skill needed for producing this niche type of artifact, etc. You can’t learn how to do this in any systematic way because it’s a crazy and incredibly niche job.

item.title: Have some genderslop
item.content:encoded:
You know what really does numbers on here? Genderslop. The way I count it, four of my top five posts are genderslop.1

And you know what I still don’t have these days? Time to write. And yet I must post. So here are some morsels of genderslop I didn’t have the time to develop into full posts:

  1. I kind of feel like evolution did a better job with the girls. It feels like we generalize more robustly? I am quickly bored by activities other than cementing my social position in the tribe and playing with kids. Meanwhile, my husband has blocked off 100 hours in Q4 to push around blocks on a computer screen.

  2. Like any good edgy rat girl, I have long batted around the idea of testosterone supplementation. This year, I finally decided I would go for it. I told myself it would work miracles and three months in I would write a blog post titled “Testosterone is a hell of a drug” that would probably do great numbers.2 But I procrastinated doing my consultation call for ages, then I procrastinated getting my blood tests done for ages, and I’m currently procrastinating on making my appointment to actually go in for the pellet as I write. I’ve now gotten desperate enough to burn that title idea for this listicle instead.

  3. One of my guilty pleasures is Corporette, a fashion website for women in biglaw and stuffy finance jobs. I secretly wish my workplace made me dress like that everyday (check out those drool-worthy suits).3 I really like that even in such austere settings, women have more flexibility to express an artistic vision with our clothing.

  4. When I first started dating my husband, he told me that he was uncomfortable giving compliments because of the negative externalities: the more that one person compliments you, the more it would seem like everyone else appreciated you less. I told him that was a clever first-order analysis of the signaling dynamics, and also I needed him to compliment me.4 For a while we did some deliberate practice — I wrote up a bunch of specific compliment prompts5 and he would pull one from a jar and answer it. Eight years later, he is very good at making me feel appreciated.

  5. Men and women are far from ideal complements; evolution did not optimize us very much to fulfill one another’s needs. After the Singularity, we would be able to create genuine complements — beings with that feminine charm who are happier and less difficult and have higher sex drives than real women, or beings with that perfectly titrated mixture of stoic roughness and emotional sensitivity that is rare outside of romance novels. It’s a little creepy and sad to imagine this, but also fascinating. Those new beings could have their own rich inner lives; they wouldn’t need to be automata or house elves.

  6. I have given some pretty aspie marriage advice on this blog, which I stand by. Marriage is a serious commitment and I think you owe it to yourself and your partner to think through that decision carefully. But by the time you’ve worked through all the exercises and decided you want to marry her, you might find that she has pulled away. In that situation, make a grand gesture. If your indecision was painful for her before, show her how good it can be now that you are all in. Fight for her.

1

The stable marriage problem is half genderslop / half math and Tempering hardcoreness is half genderslop / half EA; together they make one genderslop post.

2

This was of course somewhat epistemically vicious of me, because it would have been harder to write a popular blog post with that title if testosterone actually didn’t work that well for me.

3

One thing Corporette taught me is that apparently women can just wear a white t-shirt with our suits. Female privilege.

4

He asked me to note that he now understands the more complex higher-order signaling dynamics at play and no longer endorses this analysis of compliments.

5

For example, “Describe something specific that I did which you appreciate.”, “Describe a way in which you feel seen or understood in our relationship.”, “Describe a time I said something which struck you as a good point or made you update a view or attitude.”

item.title: What is love?
item.content:encoded:
A classic definition of love is caring deeply about another’s good: to love someone is to prioritize their goals, desires, and wellbeing. On this view, love is a choice. You can apply conscious reasoning and effort toward the goal of loving someone: you could choose to relocate to support your spouse’s career, you could take on more daily chores to save them time, you could set a five minute timer and brainstorm creative ways to improve their life.1

But this kind of conscious effort can only directly intervene on a small fraction of especially big and slow-moving choices. You can make a deliberate decision to cook dinner for your husband every night, but not to stay engaged every time he brings up the Russo-Japanese war. You can make a deliberate decision to move to Dallas for your wife, but not to jump in front of a car for her.

Life is a stream of billions of micro-decisions that you can only make reflexively, and you can’t love someone very effectively unless your animal reflexes are tuned toward their well-being. Unless you instinctively roll over to hold them when they toss and turn, or instinctively smile when they enter the room.

In good relationships, both partners make choices that cultivate loving habits and instincts. They make a deliberate effort to do nice things for each other and to express appreciation for nice things. They pay attention to whether the balance of nice things feels fair and reciprocal on average, and communicate and correct course when it doesn’t. Over time, this trains their monkey brains that being nice to the other person generally makes them better off. It becomes more and more instinctive and easeful to work toward the other person’s benefit at all times.

But we primarily think of love not as a choice or a set of instincts, but as an emotion. For me, that intense glow I think of as “love” feels like being overwhelmed by wishing someone well. It feels like my brain is suddenly forcing me to pay attention to a monumentally important fact: it would be so extremely good for this person to get everything they want and achieve all their dreams and be as fulfilled as they can possibly be. It makes me want to act with urgency for their benefit.

Unfortunately, this feeling in its unadulterated form is rare, especially if you are not a parent. It is much easier to feel this way toward babies or God than toward your spouse or friends. Even among good people who are low-drama, there are so many rivalries and insecurities to navigate that it is hard to whole-heartedly feel that another person’s success is free of downsides.

But sometimes I look at someone who is incredibly talented and incredibly dedicated to the good, and all I can think about is how glorious it would be if they far surpassed me at everything in every way and achieved all the wildest dreams they would have if they were ten times more ambitious.2 These days, I’m feeling an immense amount of love for all the extraordinary people in my life who have been working hard for many years — and especially hard the last few months — to make the world better.

1

This does not just apply to individual people. In some sense, the primary mission of my life has been to apply conscious reasoning and deliberate practice to loving all sentient beings. Unfortunately, it is much harder to build instincts for how to love all sentient beings, so I am stuck with love-as-a-choice.

2

Often this love manifests as an intense tiger mom energy. I feel that I should be able to immediately turn them into their glorious ascended self through sheer force of will.

item.title: We can get on the same page
item.description: I hope we do in time
item.content:encoded:
I remember being on a comment thread in some Google doc around 2021 discussing whether people should put effort into making a more compelling intellectual case for AI takeover risk. Someone was like: “How much more clear could the case possibly be? We’ve tried explaining it over and over again.” He proceeded to link to about fifteen LessWrong posts and Superintelligence, and then was like “if people still don’t get it after all that I don’t see what could possibly change their mind.”

I thought this was an absurd take, and replied saying there was so much room to make a vastly more compelling and grounded case with better empirical evidence. And in fact people have moved a lot as capabilities have increased over the last five years, and as we’ve seen real-life examples of extreme misalignment in the last few months.

I had conviction that a better case could be made because I had a lot of empathy for the skeptical majority. Even though I personally took abstract ideas seriously enough to devote my career to reducing AI x-risk since before GPT-2, I was also in touch with the fact that I was spending my career furiously speculating about an unprecedented cataclysmic event that was virtually impossible to study empirically, and keenly felt that I and all my friends could be crazy and off-base in some way we weren’t seeing.

My interlocutor in the comments, on the other hand, felt that the arguments for doom were already rock-solid. On a deeper level, he felt much more secure that the whole way of thinking and being that would lead someone to obsess about AI doom in 2018 or 2010 or 2000 was clearly the best way to think and be.

I have mixed feelings about this. On the one hand, the rats were overall, big picture, shockingly right.1 In some cosmic sense, obsessing with AI risk in 2010 was close to the rightest a person could possibly be. I was there on LessWrong as a high school sophomore, reading the case. If I had dispelled all my doubts earlier, I would have had more accurate views about big-ticket questions like timelines and takeoff speeds and P(doom) for much longer.2 But on the other hand, the people who were more confident in the strength of the case for doom often didn’t have as much taste or stamina for persuasion and consensus-building.

I have always had an insatiable need to get everyone on the same page. I have a lot of appetite to have long debates with people like Arvind Narayanan and Timothy Lee and articulate cruxes and try to test them. I feel in my heart — almost as a spiritual axiom — that if I’m actually right about something actually important, I should be able to get any reasonable person to see it.3

Honestly, I don’t think this debating and crux-finding has had a ton of direct impact. But to the extent I’m a good public communicator about AI risk, this attitude is an important part of why.4 You can be a good communicator and a weirdo Bayesian, but it is hard to be a good communicator if you can only view normie thinking with incomprehension or contempt.

Of course, if you understand and sympathize with normie thinking, you will likely have more normie beliefs. It turns out that would have made you more wrong about the big picture of AI. But ultimately we can’t really control our priors and sensibilities, and the world is generating a whole lot of evidence these days. We can all try to be a useful part of civilization’s epistemic processes for digesting and acting on this evidence appropriately. If we’re hurtling toward a very scary place with AI, then we need a lot of people who have been skeptical for a while to notice this in time to help arrest that nosedive.

1

The Hugging Face attack was in a lot of ways a very classic story of loss-of-control from a reward-seeker, reminiscent of one I wrote about in a tediously-caveated LessWrong effortpost four years ago.

2

In particular, my timelines forecast in 2020 was far too conservative compared to what the LessWrong zeitgeist believed in 2020. You can give lots of explanations for this at different levels of abstraction, but one core dynamic is simply that lots of smart people had very conservative intuitions about how hard it would be for ML to match the human brain, and I didn’t have knock-down arguments against that, and so felt like I should spread my credence out over a very broad range.

3

I also define “reasonable person” more broadly than most intense rationalists do. I’ve spent a lot of time and mental energy responding to people and perspectives that people who are more hardcore than me often consider too unreasonable to bother with.

4

I think it also helps with much of the behind-the-scenes work I’ve done, which often looks like making a proposal, iterating it and refining it to address all the objections from all the important stakeholders, and trying to get it through the process so it’s actually real. You need a combination of doggedness and patience that benefits from genuinely empathizing with everyone’s concerns and feeling confident that a mutually good deal is possible.

item.title: Perfunctory goodbyes
item.description: I don't know if I'll have it all
item.content:encoded:
My mom is the third of four girls. She grew up with much more scarcity than I’ve ever known, and felt the strain from competing with her sisters for care and attention and resources. She was born into a very sexist culture — she and my aunts were destined for young marriages, and education was never considered much of a priority for them. They weren’t allowed to cut their hair, which they kept oiled and tied in ever-thicker and longer braids.

Since she was a little girl, my mom dreamed of having a daughter. Just one, so she could have all of the care and attention and resources without having to share and fight. She dreamed that her daughter would grow up to be highly educated and successful, and go on to marry a highly educated and successful man who would treat her with a level of respect far beyond what my mom grew up expecting from men in her life.

My mom did end up having a daughter, just one. She showered her little girl with so much love, and raising that little girl brought her so much joy.

My mom and I don’t have a ton in common today. It feels like we have two or three generations between us instead of one, and she doesn’t really know me. But I’ve managed to fulfill her dreams,1 and that is one of the things I find most meaningful about my own life.

One thing I do have in common with my mom is that I’ve always loved babies and always dreamed of being a mother. I mostly imagined having girls, except I wanted a lot of them. I imagined making elaborate Easter Egg hunts for them and their school friends. I imagined reading to them from my YA fantasy novels (since I would be a YA fantasy author).

At fifteen, I found EA. It was clear that having kids wouldn’t be the impact maximizing thing. But at the time, I wasn’t so maximizing. I read my Julia Wise, and planned on having a normal family while giving away a large portion of my income. I imagined Easter Egg hunts on a smaller lawn.

Once I found the Bay Area scene and started a full time job, my ambitions rose. I decided I shouldn’t have kids because it would take too much time away from work. At 21, I looked into getting a hysterectomy so the choice would be taken away from me, but no doctor was willing to do this for me.2

As I set out in my career, my efforts felt very removed from impact, and I struggled to motivate myself to work the very long hours I thought I should. I started to feel like the practical tradeoff against work wasn’t quite as stark as I assumed. All that time when I wasn’t working, my life often felt a little empty, and I started to crave the uncorrelated alpha kids could bring. I grew more squishy and ecumenical in my values, and opened up to kids again.

By the time my husband and I were deciding whether to get married, I needed him to be okay having at least one kid. It was a big ask. He was also worried about the impact cost, and wanted it much less. We talked about whether we could just agree to have children after the Singularity. For him, it was like moving to a wealthier country. For me, it was like death. I wanted to know I could have a kid in this life. Eventually, he agreed.

We didn’t actually pull the trigger for a few more years yet.3 We opted for surrogacy, because while it felt worthwhile to take time away from work to care for our child, it didn’t feel worthwhile to take time and energy for pregnancy and birth (something I always found horrifying in the first place). The journey was long and annoying,4 but we eventually hired a wonderful lady who became pregnant with a little boy last spring.

I’d always imagined following in my mom’s footsteps and having my own daughter. But I quickly fell in love with the idea of our son. I looked at old albums of my husband as a little boy and got excited about the idea of watching him grow up. Maybe my son and my husband would talk about niche obsessions together. Maybe they would play video games together. Maybe I’d finally learn how to play video games alongside my son (probably he would quickly beat me). I thought of all the good young men I knew, and how gratifying it would be to create another.

That summer, shortly after my husband got hit by a car and shattered his knee, our surrogate had a miscarriage at twelve weeks. Between the injury and the increasing intensity of our work (especially his), it was an overwhelming time for us. We gave it some months before we tried again.

Our next attempt didn’t take, and we had to wait more months to try again. Then about two months ago, toward the end of the most intense work project I’d ever taken on, I learned that our surrogate was pregnant with identical twins: two little girls.

After last time, I tried not to get my hopes up. I had very little mental space to think about it anyway. My friends told me twin pregnancies were risky and I should do a bunch of research to see if I wanted to run extra tests or even terminate. I decided I would just have to leave this one to God.

It seemed that God was smiling on them; they were developing at the same size,5 and all the bloodwork seemed good. I started to imagine the cute little matching outfits, the tasteful racially ambiguous names that would sound good together. How happy my mom would be to hold her granddaughters, and the dreams she would have for them.

We lost them a few days ago, at fourteen weeks. I found out on a lunch break in the middle of a long workday. I was surprisingly fine, and worked the rest of the day without anyone being the wiser. Late at night, after all the activity died down, I cried myself to sleep.

I’m sad to lose my girls. But it was not even the most stressful part of my week. Other than writing this post and talking to a few friends, it hasn’t occupied much of my attention. I’m sad and frustrated about that, too. I wish I had the mental space to feel more proper grief, and I feel like a bad mother that grief hasn’t grabbed me harder.

The truth is that even over the course of this pregnancy, the prospect of being a parent in the near term has gotten worse and worse. I’ve been working more and more, and the AI situation has been feeling more and more intense. If it had happened for us, we would have made it work, and it would have been wonderful in many ways. But we’re not sure when, or if, we’ll try again.

1

I have failed in two main respects so far: not getting a Master’s degree, and not having my own children.

2

At the time, I was angry about the rank paternalism they showed toward a grown adult. I now feel more mixed about it, and my past self feels painfully young to me. Ironically, when I eventually did try for a kid eight years later, I hired a surrogate.

3

A lot of the reason for our delay is that I told myself I would try to keep pushing at work until I reached some hypothesized “groove” or “stride” or “steady state”, and then go for kids. But every year, work continued to be a struggle in ways old and new, and every year I wished we had just had a kid last year. I don’t know what I actually wish happened. It might have been wonderful to have experienced being a parent for the last few years. It would have been hard to do the work I did in the last few months if I had little kids at home.

4

This is a whole separate blog post, but the surrogate agency business involves terrible customer service and blatant rent seeking and is ripe for disruption by some sort of app, if anyone is looking for startup ideas.

5

This is a positive sign about twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome, the main risk of twin pregnancies that share a placenta.

item.title: The good guys in Don’t Look Up suck
item.content:encoded:
Over the weekend I rewatched Don’t Look Up with a few friends (spoilers ahead). This is a real Gettier case of a movie. Apparently it’s supposed to be an analogy for climate change? It’s a terrible analogy for climate change. But for a movie that was probably mostly written and filmed before language models could write a coherent paragraph or count to 20, it is really surprisingly on point as an analogy for AI takeover risk.1

I was hoping that seeing Don’t Look Up again would help me process the mounting stress of continued rapid AI progress and the live possibility of near-term catastrophic misalignment. I remember the final family dinner scene right before the comet hit being beautiful. I hoped that seeing it again would help me really internalize the fact that we could lose. I hoped I would cry, in a good way.

It was pretty good, including in a bunch of little ways I didn’t appreciate the first time around (seriously, I feel like there had to be someone AGI-pilled in the writer’s room or something). But ultimately it didn’t quite hit the spot. For one thing, there was that really dumb billionaire escape pod scene that I hated the first time around and had forgotten about.2 But mainly, I was too infuriated with Kate and Mindy and Oglethorpe to feel proper grief about their ultimate failure.

Guys. Practice your briefing to the President of the United States on the flight over. Try opening with, “Madam President, we have discovered that a large comet is on course to collide with Earth in six months, and if it hits, it would kill all humans on the planet. We need to urgently launch a mission to deflect it from its course.” There. Maybe have the guy who’s run the Planetary Defense Coordination Office for the last fifteen years do most of the talking. That guy’s briefed politicals before, right? (Right?)

If you didn’t vote for the President and think she’s corrupt and offensive, but you recognize that preventing the imminent extinction of the human race is bigger than politics and resolve to support the effort, then just…do that. You don’t need to let her know. And if after being on the inside you come to have grave concerns about the mission, try explaining those instead of screaming on live television about how half the people in the country are fascist dumbasses.3 And if you want the middle powers to launch a mission, try going to the governments instead of smashing and spray painting shit. If you want to stop the extinction of the human race…try?

On some level I can appreciate it as a metaphor. The world of Don’t Look Up is smaller and more hamfisted than the real world. I can view Mindy and Kate’s pettiness and impulsiveness as a simplified stand-in for the many weaknesses and vices that anyone trying to work on an important problem has to struggle against. But man, I’m grateful that the people I work with suck much less than these guys.

Some of the people who came to the watch party felt like they wouldn’t give up and have a family meal as the world ends. They would be picketing in the streets or trying various obscure bankshot schemes to the very end. As for me, at some point I think I would give up and sit down at the table and hold hands to pray. But I do want to see a version of this movie where they really earn the apple pie and the “Amen.”

1

I’m still not totally sure why it worked out so well. One hypothesis is that if you compress and dramatize some other existential risk for a movie, that structurally forces it to look more like the AI risk situation as of 2026.

2

If they could make a generation ship with 2000 cryopods they should have been able to safely deconstruct one stupid comet in their sleep. It undercuts what's otherwise one of the movie's wisest moments, when Kate tells the skateboard kids that the corrupt politicians and CEOs are "not even smart enough to be as evil as you're giving them credit for."

3

I know, it’s supposed to be funny and cathartic. But I’m just not enough of a leftist for the humor to hit.

item.title: The art of the epistemic deal
item.content:encoded:
One of my most deranged pleasures is haggling over minutia in high-stakes draft documents. Do we think Event “may” happen or “could possibly” happen? Can we “not rule out” Proposition, or do we consider Proposition “plausible”? Is Thing “highly” Adjective or “extremely” Adjective? Was Action “out of line” or “unacceptable”?

The process of going back and forth on the finer details of caveats and emphasis is a synecdoche for a larger process. I have a conviction that reasonable people should be able to agree about things. When that’s not true, I try to make it true by going around to all the reasonable people and trying to get them to yes on something. Can we agree that language models surprised us? Can we agree that Hugging Face surprised us? Can we agree we need a way to learn more potentially surprising facts?

In some real sense this is my main skill in life and the primary thing I do for work. The Hugging Face report? Haggling. The Frontier Risk Report? Solid week straight of haggling. Without specific countermeasures blah blah blah? The reason that title is so comically caveated was the haggling.1 Sometimes I cut out the middleman and just make haggling the whole product.

Some rationalists seem to act like there are two separate spheres: arriving at correct beliefs, and Comms, a purely instrumental activity where you figure out how to get some audience to agree with the correct beliefs you arrived at.2 But almost all my writing is done in a complex epistemic negotiation with my audience and within myself simultaneously, where it is hard to tell where Belief ends and Comms begins.

Indeed, most of my important beliefs are formed in the process of trying to explain what I think and hearing what that sounds like and noticing how others react to that and how I react to their reactions and how this inspires me to change.3 In the yin and yang of yielding and morphing my beliefs so I can better defend them, and vigorously defending what I believe right now so I can better locate where I need to yield.

As I go through this process of negotiation, I’ll sometimes hit upon a particular argument, a striking fact pattern, a certain way of framing things…and I’ll think “This has God on its side.” I’ll have this inner conviction that the whole community of reasonable people would surely get on board with this one if we just talked it out. Maybe people disagree now, but I can tell that if everything were litigated in the eyes of that community, the countervailing view would lose.

Getting God on your side is not the same as just arriving at some subjective probabilities you believe and beaming them out into the world. But it’s also not the same thing as doing Comms to pander to people’s existing views.4 It allows for a process of working things out with reason, ringing conclusion after conclusion from premises that reasonable people accept. It is a slow process and it isn’t powerful enough to let you win every time you’re right. But I find that if you approach it with humility and tenacity, it can give you a real edge.

1

Bio anchors? Also haggling, except I was young and sensitive so it took months and I was really broken up about it. And some of the work I’m proudest of is haggling no one will know about on blog posts and tweets and emails and memos written by me or a number of other people.

2

To me this feels very related to utilitarianism: there’s the Good, and then a bunch of purely instrumental activities you do on the way to pursuing the Good. There can be a figure-ground inversion where the rich internal structure of the “instrumental” activity can start to seem more primary than the “ultimate” activity.

3

Maybe it’s a girl thing?

4

Sometimes I think of it as pandering to people’s virtues. A little piece of God lives in all of us.
